extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral and political philosophy; those studying ethics, statesmanship, and education
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for identifying the nature of human Happiness (the chief good), the superiority of contemplative life, the requirements for moral virtue, and the role of laws, upbringing, and statesmanship in producing virtuous citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as Contemplative Speculation (theoria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness must be a kind of Contemplative Speculation: the exercise of the intellect for its own sake, continuous and self-sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Working (contemplation) is chosen for itself, yields pleasure that increases the activity, is capable of self-sufficiency and rest, and is most akin to the life of the gods; therefore the life in accordance with pure Intellect is the highest/most perfect Happiness. It also requires a sufficiently long life to attain completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity chosen for its own sake (autotelic activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true End/Happiness is an activity pursued for its own sake rather than as a means to something else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast activities of war, politics, or practical virtues (which aim at further ends like peace, power, or honors) with contemplative activity, which aims at no end beyond itself and thus better fits the criterion of being choice-worthy for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency as a criterion of Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness must be 'self-sufficient' — it completes human life and does not depend on extraneous ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-sufficiency here includes not merely the individual but the conditions that make life complete; contemplative life is most self-sufficient because it needs fewer external supports than the practical virtues, though some external goods remain necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and duration (complete life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness requires a complete duration of life — the activity must persist for an appropriately long span to be truly perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None of the points of Happiness is complete without sufficient duration; the contemplative life's continuity (uninterrupted exercise of intellect) supports its claim to be highest Happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of external goods required
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Happiness requires some external goods (health, nourishment, time), but not an excess; only a moderate supply is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External prosperity is needed to enable contemplation, but neither self-sufficiency nor virtuous action stands in excess. Moderate means can suffice for noble actions; great wealth/power are not necessary and may be irrelevant or even hindrances for contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Virtues depend on social interaction and external conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues (justice, courage, liberality, self-mastery, etc.) require people, society, opportunity, and often power or resources to be exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike contemplation, which a man of science can perform alone, practical virtues presuppose social relations (contracts, services) and conditions (temptation for self-mastery, power for brave acts), so they are less self-sufficient and often directed toward further ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom (phronesis) unites with moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom is closely united with moral excellence; moral virtues are right when they accord with Practical Wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical Wisdom supplies principles that align with virtues and is necessary for correct moral action; it belongs to the composite/human nature and helps determine what is 'befitting' in particular situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of virtuous character: nature, custom, and teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue formation arises from three sources: Nature, Custom, and Teaching; teaching and habituation are necessary but insufficient without predisposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words and precepts alone often fail to change entrenched passions; individuals need an affinity (disposition) to virtue and early habituation (right food, manner of living) for instruction to take hold. Habituation and laws help make noble behavior customary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of law and institutions in moral training
rubrics_metrics.description: Law (public institutions) should regulate upbringing, food, and manner of living because most people respond better to compulsion and punishment than to reason or honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Law has compulsory power and is a declaration from Practical Wisdom; it should employ both honour (to guide the well-disposed) and chastisement/punishments (to restrain the baser sort). In some states (e.g., Lacedæmonian) such provisions are made explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of honour and punishment in legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation should use the sense of honour to exhort those who are pliable and impose penalties tailored to be most contrary to the pleasures being pursued by wrongdoers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good laws seek to train the young by honourable examples while punishing the incurable; punishments should be chosen to counteract the particular pleasures that motivate misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private training advantages and tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Private (individual) training can better attend to particular cases and individual needs than public systems, though general principles (science) remain useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in medicine or gymnastics, private care allows tailored treatment; a competent caregiver who knows general rules and particulars can better form character in individuals, but science/general maxims remain important foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmanship/Legislation requires both practical experience and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot become a good legislator or statesman solely from compilations of laws or rhetoric; practical experience and the ability to judge what harmonises are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collections of laws are useful only to those capable of speculative judgement; those who merely gather famous laws without practical knowledge or the skill to judge and harmonise them do not thereby become legislators. Practice contributes importantly to acquiring statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws as performances/tangible results of political science
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and constitutions are the tangible products of Political Science; understanding or selecting the best laws presupposes the science and skill of legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just as physicians are not made by reading cures alone, lawmakers are not made merely by compiling successful laws; the capacity to judge and to create laws requires speculatory grasp of principles and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of opportunity to display virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression and perfection of certain virtues require appropriate external opportunities (e.g., temptation for self-mastery, power for courageous acts, money for liberality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A virtue's full exercise depends on external circumstances; many factors are required for virtuous action, and the more numerous the actions, the greater the perfection of the virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of pedagogy and rhetoric in moral reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Talking and writing alone cannot make most people virtuous; entrenched passions often resist reason and require habituation and compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetoric and precept can guide the generous youth but are powerless over those dominated by passion; successful moral education requires prior disposition, habituation, appropriate upbringing, and supportive institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy with arts/sciences: need for general principles plus case-specific judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery in legislation, like medicine or other arts, needs both general scientific principles and the judgement to apply them to particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General maxims form the object-matter of sciences and are necessary background, but skilled practitioners must also be able to treat individual cases with attention to particulars; one without the other is insufficient.
